Prehistoric describes anything that existed, happened, or was made before humans started writing things down. That's the heart of it.

Think of it this way: the word is built from two parts — pre (meaning "before") and historic (relating to recorded history). So prehistoric simply means "before recorded history."

To truly understand this word, you first need to understand what "recorded history" means, because that is the dividing line.

Human beings have been around for roughly 300,000 years. But for most of that time, people could not write. They had no alphabets, no paper, no scripts. They could not leave behind written accounts of their lives, wars, leaders, or events.

Then, about 5,000 years ago, certain civilizations — in places like ancient Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq) and ancient Egypt — began inventing writing systems. The moment a civilization started writing things down, it crossed out of prehistory and into history.

So:

  • Historic = the period for which we have written records.
  • Prehistoric = everything before those written records began.

Anything that belongs to that enormous stretch of time before writing exists is called prehistoric.

The adjective "prehistoric" can describe a wide range of things:

Creatures and animals — Any animal species that lived and died out before written history is prehistoric. Dinosaurs, woolly mammoths, saber-toothed tigers, and giant ground sloths are all prehistoric creatures. They were gone long before anyone could write about them.

Human ancestors — Early human species like Homo erectus and Neanderthals are prehistoric humans. They walked the Earth long before writing existed.

Tools and objects — A stone axe chipped by an early human thousands of years ago is a prehistoric tool. Prehistoric people made weapons, pots, and jewelry, but none of them left written instructions for how they did it.

Art — Cave paintings discovered in places like Lascaux in France or Altamira in Spain are prehistoric art. These paintings of animals and human figures are tens of thousands of years old — made long before any writing system existed.

Cultures and societies — Groups of people who lived, hunted, and built communities before writing arrived are prehistoric cultures. They had real, complex lives, but because they left no written records, we call them prehistoric.

Times and eras — You can refer to "prehistoric times" or "the prehistoric era" to mean that entire vast period of Earth's past before writing.

This is where the word becomes truly staggering in its scope.

The Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old. Life on Earth appeared roughly 3.5 billion years ago. Written history only began about 5,000 years ago.

That means virtually the entire history of life on Earth — billions of years of it — is technically prehistoric. Even most of human existence is prehistoric, since our species is 300,000 years old but writing is only 5,000 years old. We spent roughly 295,000 years being prehistoric.

An important nuance: the line between prehistoric and historic is not the same date everywhere in the world. It depends on when a particular place or culture began using writing.

Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia entered the "historic" period around 3000 BCE. But many parts of the world — in Africa, the Americas, and elsewhere — had no writing systems until much later, sometimes just a few hundred years ago. For those regions, "prehistoric" extends much further forward in time.

This means the word is always relative to a specific culture or region. A society is prehistoric until it (or someone recording it) starts writing.
How Do We Know About Prehistoric Times?

Since there are no written records, you might wonder: how do we know anything about prehistoric life at all?

Scientists and researchers piece together the prehistoric world through:

  • Fossils — preserved remains of ancient animals and plants found in rock
  • Archaeological digs — carefully excavating ancient sites to find tools, bones, and objects
  • Cave paintings and rock art — visual records left behind on cave walls
  • Ancient DNA — genetic material extracted from old bones and teeth
  • Geology — studying rock layers to understand what Earth looked like long ago

It is slow, painstaking work, but it reveals an astonishing amount about who and what came before written language.

Outside of formal or scientific contexts, people sometimes use "prehistoric" in a light-hearted or exaggerated way to describe something that feels extremely old, outdated, or out of touch with modern times — even if it isn't literally from prehistoric times.

For example:

  • "That computer is prehistoric!" — meaning it is very old and slow by today's standards.
  • "His ideas about fashion are prehistoric." — meaning they are hopelessly old-fashioned.

This is a figurative use of the word. The speaker is borrowing the sense of extreme age that "prehistoric" carries and applying it humorously to modern things. Context always makes clear whether someone means it literally or figuratively.
In a Sentence — Examples of Correct Use

• The museum displayed the skeleton of a prehistoric fish that lived 400 million years ago.
  • Archaeologists uncovered prehistoric stone tools buried beneath the city.
  • Prehistoric humans painted animals on cave walls as far back as 40,000 years ago.
  • That smartphone is so old — it's practically prehistoric! (informal)

Prehistoric means belonging to or existing in the time before humans developed writing — and it covers everything from the formation of Earth billions of years ago all the way up to the point when a given civilization first began keeping written records.
